utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, would you call the case, please, which should be included in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-10-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I also ask that the accused, Goran Jelisic, be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Nice. The Trial Chamber is going to render its decision. Let me remind you of that. The Trial Chamber is going to render its division, then you will be given the floor. First the Trial Chamber will render its decision, then you will be given the floor. The Trial Chamber is rendering its decision. You may be seated. This Trial Chamber is going to render a decision in the case the Prosecutor versus Jelisic. Let me remind you that the Prosecution, with Mr. Nice -- and I would like to say this, since you were standing before: Could you please tell us, Mr. Nice, who your colleagues are? And then I'll ask the same things of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Today I'm accompanied by Mr. Tochilovsky, who has assisted me throughout the trial; and also Mr. Bergsmo, who has been of assistance in the recent applications that have been made to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Nice. Turning to the Defence, would you introduce yourselves, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence is represented by my learned colleague, Mr. Michael Greaves, from London, and my name is Veselin Londrovic. I'm an attorney from Bijeljina. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. The Trial Chamber here, under my presidency, Claude Jorda, and working with Judge Fuad Riad and Judge Almiro Rodrigues, is going to render its decision in the case between Goran Jelisic and the Prosecutor, who was indicted for genocide and for crime against humanity and war crimes. Let me suggest that we first summarise briefly the case and then move to a presentation of the elements and arguments presented by the Prosecution. I would then suggest that I refer to the most important parts of the Judges' deliberations and, lastly, to read out the Trial Chamber's decision. A quick summary of the proceedings, and I will try to read slowly, because I know that the interpreters do not have the versions in all the languages. A brief background of the procedure. Can everybody hear me? Does the interpreters hear me? Can everybody hear me? Yes. Thank you. Goran Jelisic was initially accused of genocide, grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions, violations of the laws and customs of war, and crimes against humanity, in an indictment which was filed on the 30th of June, 1995. Goran Jelisic was arrested on the 22nd of January, 1998, and transferred immediately to The Hague. At his initial appearance on the 26th of January, 1998, he pleaded not guilty. The indictment was amended first time at the request of the Prosecutor so that all the charges based on Article 2 of the Statute for grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions were to be withdrawn, and a first amended indictment was filed on the 13th of May, 1998. Further to discussions between the parties and the Status Conference organised under the authority of the Trial Chamber by Judge Riad, an agreement on the facts relating to the pleas of guilt envisaged by Goran Jelisic was signed on 9th of the September, 1998 by the accused and by the Prosecution counsel at that time, Mr. Bowers and Mr. Tochilovsky, and Defence counsel, Mr. Londrovic, and at that time Mr. Kostic. On the basis of that agreement, a new indictment was prepared, which was filed on the 20th of October, 1998. On 29 October 1998, Goran Jelisic confirmed that he was pleading not guilty to the count of genocide. I repeat: Not guilty to the count of genocide, but did plead guilty to war crimes and crimes against humanity, as described in the agreement signed on the 9th of September. The parties agreed to consider that a trial on the crime of genocide should take place and that the hearing for the sentencing -- that is, for everything -- that is, after the genocide trial but at the time that the sentences for crimes against humanity and war crimes should then be pleaded, and it was under those conditions that the trial began. Let me now present the evidence that the Prosecutor put forth. On the 30th of November, 1998, the Prosecutor made his opening statement. He asserted that Goran Jelisic had been, and I quote, "Sent to Brcko to contribute to the campaign of ethnic cleansing," and that "For about two weeks he had acted as the principal executioner at the Luka camp. He had power over life and death" -- these are the Prosecutor's words -- "He systematically and repeatedly would kill Muslim detainees as well as certain Croats." This comes from the provisional French transcript of 30 November 1998, page 22. The Prosecutor stated that the accused had committed these murders, and again I quote, "With the intention of destroying, in whole or in part, a racial, ethnic, or religious group, and that the group targeted by Goran Jelisic was important because it included all the dignitaries of the Muslim community in Bosnia, in that region, but also by its size." "The accused" -- again, a quotation -- "demonstrated considerable authority and had received the instructions to kill the largest number of Muslims possible." For the Prosecutor, the genocidal intention could be demonstrated by the words of the accused himself, as reported by the witness -- as would be reported by the witness to the Judges, and it would appear again, quote, "That Goran Jelisic was an effective, enthusiastic participant in the genocide campaign. The Prosecutor concluded that for the Brcko victims, the face of genocide was the face of Goran Jelisic." The first Prosecution witness was heard on the 30th of November, 1998. The trial then had to be interrupted for several reasons and, in the end, was only able to resume on the 30th of August, 1999. Let me make clear that there were reasons that were outside the powers of the Trial Chamber. In all, the Prosecutor brought in 23 witnesses and presented 70 exhibits. On the 22nd of September, 1999, the Prosecutor announced to the Trial Chamber that subject to a point that it wished to bring up with the Trial Chamber, and now I quote the Prosecutor, "Yes," he said, he had reached the end of the presentation of his case, and that is the end of the quotation. Let me remind you that the point in question only dealt with the issue of knowing whether a Prosecution witness could come to confirm the statements of another Prosecution witness who had asserted that the accused had played Russian roulette with him. Other than the fact that the witness did not come forward, obviously this would not call into question the circumstance and the fact that the Prosecutor had completed the presentation of his case. At the end of the Prosecutor's statement, the Trial Chamber Judges then held a Status Conference in order to organise the Trial Chamber's work. Among other things, the Judges asked the Defence counsel whether they were planning to file a motion for rejection of the indictment. I'm saying this for the public. This is part of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence. At the end of the presentation of the evidence, a request for withdrawal of the indictment can be made. We also asked whether the accused would appear in his own defence, which is a possibility as well, a possibility which the Defence can use. After discussions, the Judges, that is, during the Status Conference, set the date of 8 November 1999 for the beginning of the presentation of the Defence case. The third part: Deliberations. The Judges then reviewed all of the evidence put forth by the Prosecution. From their deliberations, they concluded that even without having to hear the possible arguments put forth by the Defence, the accused could not be recognised as guilty of the crime of genocide. Under those conditions, the Trial Chamber asked the Registry to inform the parties that this hearing would be held in accordance with Rule 98 ter of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence in order to inform the relevant individuals that it would render its decision today in the Jelisic case. Rule 98 ter refers to decisions which can be -- judgements can be made on the basis of 98 bis, which in our Rules of Procedure and Evidence is called motion for a judgement of acquittal. Under those conditions, the Prosecutor, on the 15th of October, a few days ago, that is, filed a motion requesting that the Trial Chamber postpone its decision until the Prosecutor had had the possibility to present her arguments, particularly the legal arguments as to the status of the case. The Defence responded to that motion of the Prosecutor's today, and the Defence concluded that this motion should be rejected. The Trial Chamber considers that there is a connection, an indisociable [phoen] connection, between that request and the decision on the substance which the Trial Chamber said that it would announce its decision about today. I said to one of the parties already that the Trial Chamber had to render its decision. Therefore, there is a reason to join that motion, and we'll call that decision on the motion, to the decision on the merits. For more clarity, however, it is at that level the Trial Chamber will explain the reasons for deciding that the Prosecutor's motion must be rejected. In support of her motion, the Prosecutor put forth a set of arguments, certain of which at least partially overlap. The Prosecutor bases herself inter alia in respect of the principle audi alterem partem; that is, on the existence of a right to be heard, and on the erroneous interpretation of Rules 86(A) and 98 bis of the Rules. That is, 86(A) deals with closing arguments, and 98 bis is a request for a judgement of acquittal. Both of these articles then it put forth should be followed before the decision would be heard, and the Trial Chamber considers that this motion is inadmissible and therefore must be rejected. In the first place, it should be remembered what the letter and spirit of Rules 86 and 98 bis of the Rules are. Rule 86 provides that the Prosecutor can present a closing argument, but this is a possibility, as the text clearly states, and not an obligation. The proof for that is the circumstance that even if no final arguments are presented, the Defence may still present its argument. A Trial Chamber, therefore, is not bound to allow the Prosecutor to present closing arguments within the scope of the application of Rule 98 bis of the Rules, that is, the procedure for request for acquittal. Furthermore, the principle of audi alterem partem, according to which one must always hear the other party, could not apply to a Trial Chamber which proprio motu is acting within the framework of Rule 98 bis of the Rules. That principle which is raised by the Prosecutor does state that, save exceptions as, for example, a possibility that one party would ask to be heard ex parte; that save exceptions, the opposing party can always present a response to a motion. But in the case in point, the decision does not originate from the Defence. It was not the Defence that asked for acquittal, but it is the Trial Chamber itself, with its powers that it gets from the text; that if, after the presentation by the Prosecution of its evidence, the Trial Chamber concludes that the evidence presented is insufficient to justify a conviction for one or several of the crimes mentioned in the indictment, it will pronounce, at the request of the accused or proprio motu, acquittal. Especially, the Prosecutor is that much less entitled to present a motion by the fact that it was the Prosecutor, on the 22nd of September, stated that it completed its evidence. This is page 1681 of the French provisional transcript. In accordance with Rule 85 of the Rules, it would be logical that the moment had come for the Defence to present its own case. The Judges weighed all of the evidence which was presented by the Prosecutor, and since, at the end of the deliberations, the Judges decided, and sovereignly decided, that the evidence presented by the Prosecution was insufficient to, and I quote, "to justify a conviction," they must acquit. The text of Rule 98 bis is perfectly clear. It does not give the possibility to the Judges, under such circumstances, to acquit an accused; it obliges them to do so. The English text is just as clear, I can say for my English-speaking friends. The English text, as I said, is just as clear. "The Trial Chamber shall order the entry of a judgement of acquittal." I hope that I have not completely twisted the English language. This absolute character precludes all possibilities of intervention on the part of the accused party, except, of course, for the appeal, once the Judges have come to the decision on the basis of all of the evidence that that same party chose to present. By definition, it excludes the fact that the Prosecutor might present final arguments such as those indicated under Rule 86 of the Rules. Moreover, one must not confuse the notion of acquittal with that of lack of evidence, that is, no Prosecution case. This refers to a Prosecution argument which comes from another case which this Trial Chamber heard, that is, the Blaskic case. In the second case it is sufficient for the Trial Chamber to consider that the Prosecutor has brought in enough proof for the Defence to be in -- to have a need to answer; that is, there was a case to answer. The Defence requested that some of the charges in the Blaskic be withdrawn, so that things become set once and for all when, even if the Defence did not necessarily have the possibility of presenting even partially its exculpatory proof, the Trial Chamber does consider that there does at least exist a doubt which must redound to the benefit of the accused. In that last case, giving the Prosecutor the possibility of presenting additional evidence would be tantamount in some way of giving -- I don't like this term, but we don't have any others -- could have given a chance, an additional chance -- it's difficult to talk about chance and good luck in these dreadful circumstances -- but that would destroy the balance between the parties, or to allow her, whereas it is by definition -- the Prosecutor, by definition, constitutes the fact that the Chamber is going to render a verdict of not guilty to appeal in -- before whom? Before the same Trial Chamber -- that is, ours -- which would, of course, would be illogical and would not be consistent with the texts which have to govern the conduct of the trials. The Prosecutor cannot not also present, at the proper time, all of the proof which in its opinion would convince the Trial Chamber in order to wait for the Defence to present its own evidence. Lastly, the Prosecutor must, the Prosecutor must also know the provisions of Rule 98 bis of the Rules to prepare herself for all possible consequences, by submitting, at the proper time, to the Trial Chamber, the conclusions that -- especially the legal conclusions which the Prosecutor would consider necessary for the support of its thesis, and under these conditions Prosecutor's motion must be rejected. What is the Trial Chamber's decision? Now, I will go to that decision. Since the Trial Chamber has not heard the proof that the parties might have wanted to submit for evaluation of the penalty, that is, the sentence, and can only pronounce today a verdict of the guilt or non-guilt, and today it cannot pronounce the sentence. Moreover, the Trial Chamber has not physically had the time to draft all of the reasons for its decision, and I will explain why. The Trial Chamber must ensure an expeditious and fair trial and to permit proper administration of justice. As we have just explained, the Judges, after the deliberations as to the proof presented by the Prosecution, unanimously reached the conclusion that these elements -- I go back to 98 bis -- are insufficient to sustain a conviction on the crime of genocide. Therefore, as I said, as provided for under Rule 98 bis of the Rules, they must inproprio motu present an acquittal. But it was necessary to inform the parties thereof rapidly, and specifically the Defence, because the Defence was -- well, was to begin to present the presentation of its case on the 8th of November, and since we saw the Defence for the last time in September, this is the task the Defence was supposed to work on while thinking whether it would itself ask for an acquittal. This is proper for the proper administration of justice, to be sure that this much energy not be used in vain and to -- as soon as the Judges had finished deliberating, to be able to reach a decision. But the decision today is a public one, and I will have the occasion to go back to the right of appeal, which is open, if necessary, to the Prosecutor. Therefore, we must look through the guiding lines of what led us to this decision, which means that -- say that why -- why should we acquit Goran Jelisic of genocide and declare him, however, guilty of crimes -- of war crimes and crimes against humanity? Genocide. Reminder as regards genocide: Goran Jelisic pleaded not guilty. In order to declare an accused guilty of genocide, the Judges must not only verify the reality of the facts on which the Prosecution has based its case -- that is, in this case, the murder of several dozens of people -- but must also evaluate beyond the facts the reality of the criminal mens rea of the alleged persecutor. I'm asking the Prosecution to listen carefully here, because this perhaps is the very point which we'll be determining for the subsequent conduct of this trial. But they must also, beyond the evaluation of the facts, they must look at the reality of the criminal mens rea of the alleged perpetrator. One must be sure that the accused had or did not have the intention to destroy, in part or entirely, a national, ethnic, racial, or religious group as such. The discriminatory intention is not in and of itself sufficient, and this which distinguishes genocide from crimes of persecution, which is a crime against humanity. In order to convict an accused for genocide, one must have the proof that he had the will to destroy the discriminated group, at least in part, or at least that he had the -- he was fully conscious of the fact that he was participating, through his acts, in the commission of a genocide; that is, the destruction, at least partially, of a discriminated group. It is from the reality of this will or from this consciousness that the Judges must be convinced. From that point of view, the Trial Chamber considered it not necessary for the accused to have had the intention to perpetrate crimes over a very broad geographic area, or that he had the intention to eliminate a very substantial -- of course, it must be substantial -- part of that population, but the crimes perpetrated must show that they are perpetrators, whether he is at a high level or is simply an executor; had full conscience -- consciousness or the full desire to seek, to destroy, at least partially, a specific human group. At this point, it would perhaps be proper to go to Article 21 of the Statute, where every person is considered to be innocent until he has been proved guilty, realising that, as indicated in Rule 87 of the Rules, the guilt of the accused must be proved beyond any reasonable doubt. In the case in point, the Judges consider that the Prosecutor has not provided the sufficient proof which would allow us to establish beyond all reasonable doubt that Jelisic planned, incited, ordered, committed, or in any other way participated, in full consciousness, in the even partial destruction of the Bosnian Muslim population, as a national, ethnic, or religious group, and this doubt which must redound to the benefit of the accused. Therefore, Goran Jelisic cannot be declared guilty of genocide. We will now look at the plea of guilty. Goran Jelisic pleaded guilty to murders and physical abuse, which are characterised as crimes against humanity, respectively murders and inhumane acts; violations of the laws or customs of war, respectively murders and cruel treatment; as well as for theft qualified as war crimes, plunder. Goran Jelisic recognised that he killed at least 14 persons at the beginning of May 1992, principally at the Luka camp, where many Muslim Bosnians were detained, as well as Bosnian Croats. The accused also admitted that during that period he had committed serious physical attacks on at least four people and that he stole money from several detainees. But a plea of guilt in and of itself is insufficient in order to form the basis for the conviction of the accused. The Judges must be sure that, pursuant to Rule 62 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, that the guilty plea is made voluntarily, that the guilty plea is informed, that the guilty plea is not equivocal, and that there is sufficient factual basis for the crimes and the accused's participation in it, either on the basis of independent indicia or on a lack of any material disagreement between the parties about the facts of the case. The Trial Chamber points out that it is not important for the parties to be able to reach an agreement on the crime charged, although the Judges do have to find it -- elements within the case file on which to base their conviction, both in fact and in law, which would -- in order to say that the accused is, in fact, guilty of the crime. Preliminarily, the Trial Chamber will first recall that on the 11th of March, already the Trial Chamber ordered that -- ordered that an evaluation be carried out in order to be sure that, in light of the perceptible elements of the accused's personality and those that were provided in this respect to the Defence, that Goran Jelisic was in a position to understand the nature of the accusations against him and to follow the trial, in full knowledge of what was happening, and the experts stated that he was. Moreover, the accused, Goran Jelisic, pleaded guilty only after long discussions had taken place between the parties; that is, his Defence counsel, in the presence of the Judge; that is, the Pre-Trial Judge, Judge Riad. There was a memorandum of agreement which came as a result of that, along with its annexes, shows particularly clear the result of the discussions as to the nature and to the scope of the crimes committed by the accused. In addition, and this goes to 62 bis, testimony produced by the Prosecution during the presentation of its case amply confirmed that there was no possible doubt as to the effective commission of the acts by Jelisic, that is, acts which he recognised as being the perpetrator thereof. But Trial Chamber must still be sure that the legal characterisation given to the facts is legally founded. As regards murders and physical violence, the Trial Chamber is convinced that in this case they are not only contrary to the rights -- to the law of war and constitute violations of the laws and customs of war, but they satisfy all the legal criteria which make of them crime against humanity. The Trial Chamber, lastly, considers that the proof has been established beyond all reasonable doubt that Jelisic must be found guilty of the crime of a war of plunder for thefts that were committed against detainees in the Luka camp. Finally, the Trial Chamber -- I would like Mr. Jelisic to rise at this moment. Mr. Jelisic, would you please stand. The Trial Chamber now renders its decision. This is now the disposition of its decision, and let me remind you that the motivations for the proper intercession of justice will be given subsequently. The Trial Chamber acquits you of the count of genocide -- that was Count 1 of the indictment -- declares that you are guilty of Counts 4 to 23, 30 to 33, 36 to 41, for crimes against humanity, murder, and inhumane acts, and violations of the laws or customs of war, murder, cruel treatment, and plunder; and guilty of Count 44, plunder, a violation of the laws or customs of war, states that the time period provided for in Rule 108 of the Rules, in order to appeal this decision, will start to run as of today, but that the time period provided for under the relevant Articles of the Rules in order to set up an appeals file case will begin to run only starting from that point when the Trial Chamber has rendered its reasons -- decision in writing, and states that Goran Jelisic will remain in detention at least until the Trial Chamber has rendered its decision. You may be seated. You may be seated now. The Trial Chamber will now hold a Status Conference after a brief suspension, in order to set up a schedule for the possible presentation by the parties of anything that they wish to put forth in respect of the sentencing. The Court now stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
